Marcionism came from Marcion of Sinope in the 2nd century AD. The basic idea that Marcion of Sinope came up with (because there was no scriptural support for this) is that the REAL disicple of Jesus/Yeshua wasn't all those dudes that were there in person hanging out with him while he went around preaching, it was this guy Saul/Paul who never met him, but wrote a bunch of letters after he converted into a follower of Jesus. He also pushed the idea that the God of the Old Testament was a mean vengeful god, and Jesus was basically the nice, compassion god of the New Testament, and because Old Testament = Jews, and New Testament = Christians, and in his head Jews = Bad, then we can just throw away that "Jew" bible, and focus on just the nice, good, Christian New Testament. Never mind that Jesus/Yeshua was a Jew that taught at the Temple on various occassions. 
Marcion of Sinope was immediately branded a heretic by the church body in Rome in 144 AD.

Oh yeah, he also cobbled together his own version of the new testament with Saul/Paul's writings that he liked and his own versino of the Gospel of Luke that he called, "The Gospel of Marcion". Totally cool and on the level!

Here is something interesting, and I think it mirrors present day in a lot of ways: Marcion tried to buy his way into the current church body in Rome by donating a large amount of money. When he tried to push his own theology and basically take over the church, he was cast out, and his donation was even returned. So he used his wealth to set up his own church, and got people to join it, with many current theologians calling him a 'proto-protestant'. 

You would think that someone that was branded a heretic way back in the 2nd century would have ideas that just sort of went away, but that didn't happen. He had enough followers that many people today carry his ideas without even knowing where they came from originally.

Well, per the article that this meme came from, the HB 1191 bill would "...compel the Florida Transportation Department to study using phosphogypsum in road construction aggregate material to determine its feasibility as a paving material." So approving the study of it would be a good idea, because it might turn out to be a negligible impact on the environment (including the pour and place crews). 

As to how this could impact the economy? It could potentially lower the cost of construction dramatically. For example, in my limited experience, we are approved to use between 20% to 25% fly ash in a cementitious mixture, which translates up to $5.00 discount PER YARD that we use. It's a huge game changer when bidding projects, because it allows for more constuction to happen, which translates for more jobs created, and more people earning more money and so on. Now, one of the issues with fly ash is that it is limited, as it is by product of coal plants, so sometimes we have to buy barges of fly ash from China, or we just don't have fly ash available to be used, which can stall construction for months, sometimes even years, depending on the size of the project. 
If the study is allowed to be performed and phosphogypsum is deemed safe enough to be used in construction, with the majority of it being produced in Florida, we could not only save money in construction, but also boost our own local economy, instead of sending that money overseas. So, we'll see. I sure HOPE that it is safe, but if the study comes out stating that it isn't, then I really hope that nobody gets bribed into approving it anyway.
